q: So what do we actually know?
answer: Your question — what we actually know — is broader than what this shelf carries. Four distinct sources speak here, and the shelf shows few. Here is what they say, plainly. The 'spirituality as a thing one has' framing — displayed, compared, ranked — is an observation about the culture round the texts, not a datum out of any of them. The texts speak of practice and responsibilities; the culture speaks of status. Family and work remain, and no text here says they do not. The Gita 18.7 parts the surrender that flees from the surrender that lets go the thirst for the result. Sacrifice, gift, and austerity are not to be dropped — they are to be done — so that not-clinging is no longer not-doing, and the responsibility for the act stands. That the mind-precedes of the Dhammapada and the neti-neti of the Brihadaranyaka are one doctrine of mind is a reading neither text says. The reality they are said to meet at is our part of the sentence, not the texts'. The Gita 17.2-3 distinguishes the faiths by the three gunas — the stead and single, the fervent and craving, the drifting and lost. A person's nature makes their faith. Desire, fear, and anger are named as the gates that unseat a person, so the discernment asked is of the cast of the source, not the heat of the feeling. (as a guard-note of ours, on records 5 and 6 has it) (as modern spiritual culture (our own description) has it)

q: How do I know if I'm actually experiencing it?
answer: Your question — whether you're actually experiencing it — is broader than what this shelf carries. Four distinct sources speak here, and the shelf shows few. Here is what they say around the shape of your asking. The culture round the texts makes spirituality a thing one HAS — displayed, compared, ranked. If you are checking whether you are 'actually' having the experience, you may already be in that frame. The texts speak of practice and responsibilities, not of a status you confirm. Family and work remain, and no text here says they do not. Cook Ting's blade lasts nineteen years because it moves in the seams and never strikes the great bones. 'I follow the natural pattern, I work by the natural pattern, and my blade is as if newly set.' The sign the text names is not a grand confirmation. It is that the work continues, that the thing is nursed. If the yielding is there, the blade is still sharp. And you cannot pin the experience to a definition the way you'd pin a doctrine. Consciousness has no agreed definition; the instruments have not spoken either way. The reality you think the texts meet at may be your part of the sentence, not theirs. So the 'actually' you are reaching for may not be a fact the shelf can hand you. (as modern spiritual culture (our own description) has it) (as philosophy of mind, our state of the question has it)
